titleBlock.headline: Trametinib + Rapamycin Combine Additively to Extend Mammalian Lifespan by Up to 34.9%
titleBlock.authors: Gkioni, L., Nespital, T., Baghdadi, M., Monzó, C., Bali, J., Hendrich, O., Patil, S., Beyer, A., Grönke, S. & Partridge, L.
titleBlock.summary: By simultaneously targeting both arms of the insulin/IGF-1/growth factor signaling network—mTORC1 via intermittent rapamycin (42 mg/kg diet alternate weeks) and the Ras–MEK–ERK cascade via continuous trametinib (1.44 mg/kg diet)—in 875 C3B6F1 hybrid mice from 6 months of age, Gkioni & Partridge achieved truly additive lifespan extension (+34.9% female median, +27.4% male median) alongside liver/spleen tumor suppression and complete blockade of age-related brain glucose hypermetabolism.

studyOverview.title: The Question
studyOverview.content: Downstream of growth factor and insulin/IGF-1 receptors, signaling bifurcates into the PI3K–Akt–mTORC1 branch and the Ras–MEK–ERK branch. Does inhibiting MEK1/2 with the FDA-approved oncology drug trametinib extend mammalian lifespan on its own, and does combining it with mTORC1 inhibition (rapamycin) produce additive longevity and healthspan gains?

studyOverview.title: What They Did
studyOverview.content: Randomized n = 875 genetically identical F1 hybrid mice (C3B6F1, both males and females, ~100–121 mice per sex per arm) starting at 6 months of age into 4 arms: Control diet, Trametinib alone (1.44 mg/kg diet continuous), Rapamycin alone (42 mg/kg diet intermittent every other week), and Combined Trametinib + Rapamycin, paired with longitudinal 18F-FDG PET/CT brain imaging, histopathology, and multi-tissue RNA-seq.

studyOverview.title: What They Found
studyOverview.content: Trametinib alone extended median lifespan by +7.2% (♀) and +10.2% (♂) without causing glucose intolerance. Rapamycin alone extended median lifespan by +17.4% (♀) and +16.6% (♂). Remarkably, the combination additively extended median lifespan by +34.9% in females (maximum +32.4%) and +27.4% in males (maximum +26.1%), while uniquely reducing liver/spleen tumors and blocking age-related brain neuroinflammation and glucose hypermetabolism.

arms.label: Untreated Control
arms.brainPetChange: +11.5% to +14% pathological age-related rise in striatum/cortex 18F-FDG uptake from 12 to 24 mo
arms.liverTumorRate: Baseline high incidence of late-life liver & spleen neoplasia at 24 mo
arms.microgliaStatus: High Iba-1+ activated microglia & GFAP+ reactive astrocytes at 24 mo

arms.label: Trametinib Monotherapy
arms.glucoseEffect: Neutral (No hyperglycemia, no insulin resistance, normal AST/ALP liver enzymes)
arms.brainPetChange: Partially attenuated age-related rise in brain glucose uptake
arms.liverTumorRate: Modest non-significant trend toward lower tumor burden
arms.microgliaStatus: Moderate reduction in striatal microglia density in females

arms.label: Rapamycin Monotherapy
arms.regimen: 42 mg/kg Diet Intermittent (Alternate Weeks, mTORC1 Inhibitor)
arms.glucoseEffect: Mild glucose intolerance (elevated GTT AUC due to partial mTORC2 sensitivity)
arms.brainPetChange: Partially attenuated age-related brain glucose hypermetabolism
arms.liverTumorRate: Did not significantly reduce 24-month liver tumor prevalence alone
arms.microgliaStatus: Reduced splenic enlargement and systemic pro-inflammatory cytokines

arms.label: Trametinib + Rapamycin
arms.regimen: 1.44 mg/kg Continuous Trametinib + 42 mg/kg Alternate-Week Rapamycin
arms.glucoseEffect: No exacerbation of rapamycin glucose effect; normal liver transaminases (AST/ALP)
arms.brainPetChange: 100% Blockade: Completely prevented age-related 18F-FDG hypermetabolism across striatum, cortex & cerebellum
arms.liverTumorRate: Significant reduction in 24-month liver tumors (♀ & ♂) and male spleen tumors
arms.microgliaStatus: Synergistic suppression of Iba-1+ microglia, GFAP+ astrocytes & renal/splenic inflammation

doseOptimizationNote: Crucial Dose-Window Discovery: In preliminary dosing trials, high doses of trametinib (5.76 and 11.52 mg/kg diet) caused weight loss, hepatic/splenic pathology, and shortened male lifespan. Titrating down to 1.44 mg/kg diet (~0.24 mg/kg/day body weight—roughly 10-fold below oncology dosing, achieving ~2.8 ng/mL plasma levels) unlocked clean lifespan extension without hematological or hepatic toxicity.

transcriptomics.detail: Over 80% of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the combined treatment arm were unique to the combination rather than present in single-drug arms—downregulating canonical NF-κB, IL-6/JAK/STAT3, complement cascade, and chemokine signaling while preserving mitochondrial OXPHOS.

In aged brains, pro-inflammatory microglia consume excessive glucose via aerobic glycolysis, driving an age-related surge in 18F-FDG PET signal. Dual MEK1/2 + mTORC1 blockade silenced microglial/astrocytic activation, keeping 24-month brain glucose metabolism indistinguishable from 12-month-old mice.

Longitudinal ECG and open-field monitoring showed that combined therapy blunted the age-related decline in resting heart rate, prevented pathological QT-interval prolongation at 24 months, and increased voluntary exploratory locomotion in aged mice.

keyFindings.title: First Mammalian Lifespan Extension by a Clinical MEK1/2 Inhibitor
keyFindings.desc: Extends the Partridge Lab's earlier 2015 Drosophila discovery (Slack et al., Cell) into mammals: low-dose trametinib (1.44 mg/kg) extended mouse median lifespan by +7.2% (♀) and +10.2% (♂) and male maximum lifespan by +15.8%.

keyFindings.title: True Additive Synergy (+34.9% ♀ / +27.4% ♂ Median Lifespan)
keyFindings.desc: Inhibiting both Ras–MEK–ERK and PI3K–mTORC1 branches of the nutrient/growth-factor network nearly doubled the lifespan benefit of intermittent rapamycin alone, pushing female maximum lifespan up by +32.4%.

keyFindings.title: Complete Blockade of Aged Brain Glucose Hypermetabolism (18F-FDG PET)
keyFindings.desc: Contrary to human Alzheimer's hypometabolism, normal mouse brain aging exhibits glial-driven hyper-glycolysis (+11.5–14% FDG uptake from 12 to 24 mo); only the dual therapy completely abolished this neuroinflammatory metabolic shift.

keyFindings.title: Narrow Therapeutic Window Requires Sub-Oncology Microdosing
keyFindings.desc: Whereas 5.76–11.52 mg/kg trametinib was toxic in males, 1.44 mg/kg (~2.8 ng/mL plasma concentration, well below the ~5.5–22 ng/mL human melanoma therapeutic range) was completely free of liver or metabolic toxicity.

conclusions.title: Poly-Pathway Network Targeting Overcomes Single-Drug Ceilings
conclusions.content: Because insulin/IGF-1 and receptor tyrosine kinases signal through parallel PI3K–mTORC1 and Ras–MEK–ERK cascades with cross-compensatory feedback, dual inhibition achieves a magnitude of mammalian lifespan extension (+34.9%) rarely seen outside radical genetic dwarfism or severe caloric restriction.

conclusions.title: Intermittent Rapamycin + Continuous Low-Dose MEK Inhibition
conclusions.content: Delivering rapamycin intermittently (every other week) captured its full geroprotective benefit (~17% median extension) while pairing seamlessly with continuous low-dose trametinib without compounding metabolic side effects.

conclusions.title: Convergent Link with Anti-IL-11 Longevity Signaling
conclusions.content: This study provides direct mechanistic synergy with Widjaja et al. (Nature 2024, Anti-IL-11), which demonstrated that age-related IL-11 signals precisely through the ERK–mTORC1 axis to drive multi-organ senescence and fibrosis.

protocolImplications: Translational context: Both rapamycin (sirolimus) and trametinib (Mekinist) are FDA-approved human pharmaceuticals with extensive clinical pharmacology profiles. However, oncology doses of trametinib (2 mg/day in humans) cause significant rash, cardiomyopathy, and ocular toxicity. Gkioni et al. demonstrate that geroprotective efficacy in mammals occurs at roughly 1/5th to 1/10th of the oncology exposure (~2.8 ng/mL plasma), establishing a roadmap for ultra-low-dose combinatorial geroprotector clinical trials.
